{{Short description|Set function that is a precursor to a measure}}
In [[mathematics]], a '''pre-measure''' is a [[set function]] that is, in some sense, a precursor to a ''[[bona fide]]'' [[Measure (mathematics)|measure]] on a given space. Indeed, one of the fundamental theorems in measure theory states that a pre-measure can be extended to a measure.

==Definition==
Let <math>R</math> be a [[Ring of sets|ring of subsets]] (closed under [[union_(set_theory)|union]] and [[relative complement]]) of a fixed set <math>X</math> and let <math>\mu_0 : R \to [0, \infty]</math> be a [[set function]]. <math>\mu_0</math> is called a '''pre-measure''' if 
<math display=block>\mu_0(\varnothing) = 0</math>
and, for every [[countable set|countable (or finite) sequence]] <math>A_1, A_2, \ldots \in R</math> of [[pairwise disjoint]] sets whose union lies in <math>R,</math>
<math display=block>\mu_0 \left(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n\right) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mu_0(A_n).</math>
The second property is called [[sigma additivity|<math>\sigma</math>-additivity]].

Thus, what is missing for a pre-measure to be a measure is that it is not necessarily defined on a [[sigma-algebra]] (or a [[sigma-ring]]).

==Carathéodory's extension theorem==
{{main|Carathéodory's extension theorem}}

It turns out that pre-measures give rise quite naturally to [[outer measure]]s, which are defined for all subsets of the space <math>X.</math>  More precisely, if <math>\mu_0</math> is a pre-measure defined on a ring of subsets <math>R</math> of the space <math>X,</math> then the set function <math>\mu^*</math> defined by
<math display=block>\mu^* (S) = \inf \left\{\left. \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \mu_0(A_i) \right| A_i \in R, S \subseteq \bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty} A_i\right\}</math>
is an outer measure on <math>X</math> and the measure <math>\mu</math> induced by <math>\mu^*</math> on the <math>\sigma</math>-algebra <math>\Sigma</math> of [[Carathéodory-measurable set]]s satisfies <math>\mu(A) = \mu_0(A)</math> for <math>A \in R</math> (in particular, <math>\Sigma</math> includes <math>R</math>). The infimum of the empty set is taken to be <math>+\infty.</math>

(Note that there is some variation in the terminology used in the literature.  For example, Rogers (1998) uses "measure" and "pre-measure" where this article uses terms "outer measure" and "set function", respectively.  Outer measures are not, in general, measures, since they may fail to be <math>\sigma</math>-additive.)
